                                            I.    INTRODUCTION

        Pursuant to 10 C.F.R. § 2.311(b), NextEra Energy Duane Arnold, LLC (“NextEra”) files

this answer and brief in opposition to Physicians for Social Responsibility Iowa’s (“PSRI” or

“Petitioner”) appeal (“Appeal”) 1 of the Atomic Safety and Licensing Board’s (“Board” or

“ASLB”) decision in LBP-26-9. 2 In that decision, the Board denied PSRI’s hearing request and

petition to intervene (“Petition”) 3 and terminated the contested proceeding after concluding that

each of PSRI’s five proposed contentions was inadmissible. In its Appeal, PSRI seeks reversal

of the Board’s holdings on two of those contentions. 4

        As an initial matter, the Commission need not reach the substance of either admissibility

ruling because PSRI’s Appeal fails at the threshold on both contentions. For whatever reason,

PSRI left unchallenged the single holding that independently defeats each contention. As a

matter of law, an appeal that does not confront the dispositive basis for the ruling below presents

no error of law or abuse of discretion to review.

        On Contention 3, which asserted that the NRC lacks authority to authorize the restart of a

previously shutdown reactor, PSRI’s Appeal does not even allege that the Board erred. To the

contrary, PSRI concedes that the Commission’s Palisades decision (CLI-26-7) 5 forecloses the

contention and that the Board was bound to reject it. PSRI merely asks the Commission to

PSRI offers no argument whatsoever that CLI-26-7 was wrongly decided or should be revisited.

A request to preserve an issue, unaccompanied by any argument for a different result, abandons

it. There is nothing for the Commission to correct.

        In Contention 5, PSRI argued that the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969

(“NEPA”) mandated an environmental analysis of a nearby private data center project and that

NextEra committed a “segmentation” error by excluding such analysis from its Environmental

Report (“ER”). But PSRI’s Appeal does not confront the Board’s threshold ruling that the

contention is immaterial under 10 C.F.R. § 2.309(f)(1)(iv). Specifically, the Board held that,

notwithstanding PSRI’s allegation of error, PSRI failed to address the alleged magnitude

(i.e., materiality) of that error. That is the independent, overarching ground on which the Board

rejected all of PSRI’s NEPA contentions—including Contention 5. But the Appeal only

addresses five “additional considerations” articulated by the Board, in a different part of

LBP-26-9, explaining several other reasons why Contention 5 was inadmissible. Where a

contention is rejected on multiple independent grounds and the appellant challenges only some,

the unchallenged ground stands and is alone sufficient to affirm. PSRI’s failure to engage the

materiality holding is, by itself, dispositive.

        Only if the Commission looks past this threshold defect would it reach PSRI’s

substantive arguments on Contention 5. But doing so would compel the same result. The Board

faithfully applied the Supreme Court’s decision in Seven County, 6 which holds that an agency

need not analyze the environmental effects of a project it has no authority to regulate. The NRC

licenses reactors, not data centers, so the Board correctly rejected PSRI’s claim that NEPA

 mandates environmental analysis of a separate, privately owned data center project. PSRI’s

segmentation and related theories identify no error in that conclusion. Under the substantial

AFFIRM LBP-26-9.

                                           II.    BACKGROUND

A.       Procedural History

         This proceeding concerns the Duane Arnold Energy Center (“DAEC”). In 2020, DAEC

was shutdown, defueled, and its license amended to disallow the loading of fuel into the reactor. 7

Those steps reflected plans to eventually decommission DAEC, but did not terminate its

Renewed Facility Operating License (which only occurs after decommissioning is complete). In

January 2025, NextEra decided to pursue a restart of power operations at DAEC, submitting an

exemption request shortly thereafter, 8 and later filing three license amendment requests

(“LARs”) 9 in connection with the proposed restart.

         On April 22, 2026, the Commission published a notice providing interested persons an

opportunity to request a hearing on the three LARs. 10 To obtain a hearing, petitioners must

         In LBP-26-9, the Board concluded that PSRI had established representational standing. 18

However, the Board held that none of PSRI’s five contentions satisfied the admissibility

requirements of 10 C.F.R. § 2.309(f)(1); accordingly, it denied PSRI’s hearing request and

terminated the proceeding. 19

         As pertinent to the instant Appeal, the Board rejected Contention 3 because binding

Commission precedent in the Palisades restart proceeding foreclosed PSRI’s challenge; in its

to raise in this case. 20 As to each of PSRI’s NEPA contentions (including Contention 5), the

 Contention 3 before the Board; but, instead of challenging that precedent, PSRI uses the Appeal

NextEra timely files this answer and brief in opposition to the Appeal.

B.       Standard of Review for Appeals

         A licensing board decision denying a hearing request “is appealable by the

requester/petitioner on the question as to whether the request and/or petition should have been

granted.” 26 The Commission’s longstanding practice is to afford substantial deference to a

licensing board’s rulings on standing and contention admissibility. 27 Additionally, the

Commission will “generally leave to the Board’s judgment whether a proposed contention has a

sufficient factual basis to be admitted for hearing.” 28 Therefore, an appeal challenging a

licensing board’s threshold determination on contention admissibility that identifies no error of

law or abuse of discretion, but merely repeats prior arguments and disagreement with the

licensing board’s decision, does not warrant reversal. 29

          Given the “high standard of review,” 30 a petitioner has a “heavy burden” on appeal to

establish that reversal of a licensing board’s decision is warranted. 31 As the Commission has

previously stated, “[t]he appellant bears the responsibility of clearly identifying the errors in the

decision below and ensuring that its brief contains sufficient information and cogent argument to

alert the other parties and the Commission to the precise nature of and support for the appellant’s

claims.” 32

                       III.   THE COMMISSION SHOULD AFFIRM LBP-26-9

         PSRI appeals the Board’s admissibility rulings on Contention 3 and Contention 5.

However, PSRI identifies no error of law or abuse of discretion—or any other reason to disturb

the Board’s decision. Simply put, PSRI’s Appeal fails as to both contentions for the exact same

reason: PSRI never engaged the dispositive holding for either one. As further explained below,

the Commission should affirm LBP-26-9.

A.       On Contention 3, PSRI Fails to Present a Valid Appeal

         In Contention 3, PSRI purported to challenge NextEra’s LARs because “there is no

dedicated regulatory procedure for restarting a closed reactor,” and therefore “the NRC has no

authority to approve the license amendments requested by NextEra.” 33 But, as PSRI

acknowledges, the Commission recently rejected an “identical” 34 argument in a different

proceeding. More specifically, in the Palisades restart proceeding, the Commission conducted a

de novo legal review and affirmed a licensing board ruling “rejecting [petitioners’] arguments

     n.25 (2004) (quoting Advanced Med. Sys., Inc. (Geneva, OH), CLI-94-6, 39 NRC 285, 297 (1994)).

 that our existing regulatory processes cannot be used to restore a decommissioning reactor to

operations,” stating that the licensing board’s ruling is “consistent with the NRC’s longstanding

interpretation of the regulations.” 35 The Commission’s published decision, CLI-26-7, explained

that “the existing regulations provide a process to allow for the resumption of operations at a

reactor that has submitted the § 50.82(a) certifications and permanently shut down.” 36 PSRI

“agreed” that CLI-26-7 is controlling authority that squarely contradicts PSRI’s legal theory of

Contention 3, and it “concedes” that the Board was obligated to follow that binding precedent in

rejecting Contention 3 as inadmissible. 37

          On appeal, PSRI now states that it “objects to the ASLB’s ruling.” 38 But PSRI offers

nothing more. PSRI neither claims an error of law or abuse of discretion in LBP-26-9 nor

explains any reason why the Commission should overturn its holding in CLI-26-7. That

approach is manifestly inadequate. A document purporting to be an appeal that “points to no

error of law or abuse of discretion on the part of the Board,” 39 is insufficient to satisfy the

Commission’s “requirements for a valid appeal,” and should be summarily denied. 40 That is the

case here. The Appeal points to no error of law or abuse of discretion. In fact, PSRI concedes

that the Board correctly followed binding precedent, which forecloses any showing of error.

          To be clear, PSRI’s arguments to the Board made no attempt to distinguish Contention 3

from the arguments considered—and rejected—by the Commission in CLI-26-7. Nor did PSRI

present even a single theory about how or why the Commission’s holding in CLI-26-7 is

 incorrect. In fact, PSRI did not disclose or confront CLI-26-7 in its Petition at all. Even after

that failure was highlighted in the answer pleadings filed by the other parties, PSRI’s Reply did

not engage with the holding or reasoning in CLI-26-7. Quite simply, PSRI made no genuine

effort to obtain a different result. For that self-created reason, there is no error of law or abuse of

discretion to which PSRI could point in its Appeal. And because the Appeal does not, in fact,

allege Board error, PSRI has not met the standard of review for administrative appeals.

         At the Board level, the restart authority issue was genuinely governed by CLI-26-7. The

Board “agree[d] with all participants that the admissibility of Contention 3 is foreclosed by

Commission precedent,” and PSRI itself “concede[d] that this Board’s hands are tied by the

Commission’s prior decision.” 41 That concession was correct at the Board level. However, the

instant Appeal under § 2.311 is presented to the Commission, which authored CLI-26-7 and

could reconsider it (but PSRI gave it no reason to). An agency “is not precluded from

announcing new principles in an adjudicative proceeding.” 42 Agencies are “free to change their

existing policies.” 43 And the Commission has, in fact, reconsidered, overruled, or reversed its

own adjudicatory precedent in other past proceedings. 44 This Appeal before the Commission

         PSRI’s Appeal also continues to press its claim that failure to evaluate the data center

more parts so as to disperse the environmental effects among different federal projects. 82 Here,

federal project and a separate, nonfederal project.

automatically require the agency to evaluate the “environmental effects of that separate
